fatal_errors: The as-deposited material is incorrectly described as an ordered hexagonal phase with a first-order magnetostructural transition; the target films and nanoribbons were amorphous or extremely fine/disordered with only cubic-type short-range order.

The proposed annealing mechanism requires grain refinement and second-phase precipitation, whereas the relevant 700 K treatment produced neither detectable crystallization nor phase separation and instead caused short-range atomic reordering and internal-strain relaxation.
Annealing is generally not a credible route to grain-size reduction without an additional recrystallization or deformation mechanism.

The predicted transition broadening and hysteresis reduction do not reconstruct the observed outcomes: increased magnetization and a modest increase in peak magnetic entropy change near 140 K while retaining the pre-crystallization structure.
The cited evidence concerns unrelated refractory and AlCoFeNi/AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys and does not support the claimed magnetocaloric mechanism in FeMnNiGeSi films.
explanation: The response recognizes post-deposition annealing as a controllable intervention and gives an operational falsification test, but it imports the ordered, first-order-transition behavior of bulk material into the wrong as-deposited thin-film baseline. Its central mediator—precipitate-bearing, grain-refined heterogeneity—is opposite to the observed structural invariance at 700 K. It also omits the relevant nanoribbon geometry, spacing-dependent coupling, elastic-strain intervention, temperature and field ranges, amorphous pre-crystallization boundary, and inverse low-temperature response. The proposed experiment could test its own heterogeneity hypothesis, but varying annealing temperature and time simultaneously with microstructural evolution would not cleanly separate precipitation effects from strain relaxation, short-range ordering, or crystallization.
